revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Presidential Terms
revealWordProblem.text: A presidential term in the United States is four years. In 1947, Congress passed an amendment to limit the president to two terms. The number of terms served by each president of the United States from 1789 to 2021 is shown in the bar graph. Given this information, what prediction can you make about the number of terms the next U.S. president will serve in office?
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The bar graph shows: less than 1 term = 7 presidents, 1 term = 18, between 1 and 2 terms = 3, 2 terms = 15, more than 2 terms = 1. That's 7 + 18 + 3 + 15 + 1 = 44 presidents total. The tallest bar, and the mode of the data, is '1 term' with 18 out of 44 presidents, or 18 ÷ 44 ≈ 0.409 = 40.9% — the largest share of any category. Also, since the 1947 amendment now caps presidents at two terms, 'more than 2 terms' is no longer possible for future presidents. Based on this data, the most likely prediction is that the next U.S. president will serve 1 term.

onLevel.stem: A baseball player's batting averages over 6 seasons are: .280, .295, .290, .285, .300, .110. The .110 was an injury-shortened season. Which measure better represents the player's typical batting average?
choices: Median, because the .110 outlier pulls the mean down
Mean, because it uses all the data
Mean, because .110 is a real season
Neither measure works
onLevel.explanation: The .110 is an outlier that pulls the mean down to .260. The median (.2875) better represents typical performance because it isn't affected by the extreme value.
choiceFeedback: Mean uses all data—but the .110 outlier pulls it down.
Even though .110 is real, which measure shows typical performance better?
Both measures exist, but which resists the .110 outlier?
hints: Five seasons sit between .280 and .300; the .110 season is far below them — a low outlier.
A low outlier drags one measure DOWN below the player's usual level. Think about which measure uses only the middle of the ordered list.
First step: order the six averages and find the two middle ones. Notice that .110 sits at the far end and never touches that middle.
onLevel.stemEs: Los promedios de bateo de un jugador en 6 temporadas son: .280, .295, .290, .285, .300, .110. El .110 fue una temporada acortada por lesión. ¿Cuál medida representa mejor el promedio de bateo típico del jugador?
onLevel.explanationEs: El .110 es un valor atípico que baja la media hasta .260. La mediana (.2875) representa mejor el rendimiento típico porque no se ve afectada por el valor extremo.

onLevel.title: Spot the Mistake — Choosing the Mean Despite an Outlier

workedExample.label: Data
workedExample.work: A receiver's catches per game: 12, 14, 13, 15, 11, 60 (the 60 was a record-setting playoff game).

workedExample.label: Choose a measure
workedExample.work: The student reports the mean (≈ 20.8) as the typical number of catches because it uses every game.

onLevel.correctWork: The student should report the median (13.5), not the mean. The 60-catch game is an outlier that pulls the mean up to about 20.8 — higher than 5 of the 6 games. The median (13.5) is resistant to that outlier and better represents a typical game.
hints: Compare the mean (≈ 20.8) to the actual games. Is it close to a typical value, or higher than almost all of them?
When one value (60) is far from the rest, it pulls the mean. The median (13.5) stays near the cluster, so it is the better choice.
onLevel.titleEs: Detecta el error: elegir la media a pesar de un valor atípico
onLevel.explanation: Using every value is exactly the problem here: the 60-catch playoff game pulls the mean up to about 20.8, which is higher than five of the six games. The median 13.5 sits inside the cluster of 11 to 15 and is not moved by that extreme value, so it is the better report of a typical game.
onLevel.explanationEs: Usar todos los valores es justo el problema aquí: el partido de playoffs con 60 recepciones sube la media hasta cerca de 20.8, más alto que cinco de los seis partidos. La mediana 13.5 queda dentro del grupo de 11 a 15 y ese valor extremo no la mueve, así que representa mejor un partido típico.

onLevel.title: Find the Reasoning Error

workedExample.label: Conclusion
workedExample.work: The mean (28.2) is the best measure because it uses all the data.

onLevel.correctWork: The median (32.5) is the better measure. The value 5 is an outlier (the player was injured that game) that pulls the mean down to 28.2, which is lower than any of the player's healthy games. The median (32.5) better represents typical minutes played.
hints: Look at the value 5. Does it fit with the rest of the data?
The mean (28.2) is lower than 5 of the 6 values. Does that seem like a 'typical' game?
onLevel.explanation: The value 5 is an outlier from an injury game, and it drags the mean down to 28.2 — lower than every healthy game in the set. The median 32.5 sits among the 30-to-35 minute games, so it describes typical minutes far better. Using all the data is not an advantage when one value is that extreme.
onLevel.explanationEs: El valor 5 es un valor atípico de un partido con lesión, y jala la media hasta 28.2, más bajo que cualquier partido sano del conjunto. La mediana 32.5 queda entre los partidos de 30 a 35 minutos, así que describe mucho mejor los minutos típicos. Usar todos los datos no es una ventaja cuando un valor es así de extremo.

onLevel.prompt: A local newspaper reports that the average home price in a neighborhood is $450,000. The actual prices are: $180K, $200K, $190K, $210K, $195K, $1,725K. Is the reporter's claim misleading? Calculate the mean and median and explain which better represents a 'typical' home price.
onLevel.sentenceFrame: Mean = ___. Median = ___. The reporter's claim is ___ because the outlier ($1,725K) pulls the mean ___. The ___ (about $___) better represents a typical home price because ___.
onLevel.hint: Start by calculating both the mean and median—compare them to see if an outlier pulled mean.
hints: Five homes cost about $180K–$210K; one costs $1,725K. Check the reporter's $450,000 'average' against those five real prices.
Plan: (1) mean = sum of all six prices ÷ 6, (2) median = average of the 3rd and 4th ordered prices, (3) compare each to what most homes cost.
Step 1: add 180 + 200 + 190 + 210 + 195 + 1725 (in thousands) and divide by 6. Then order the six prices and average the middle two.
onLevel.explanation: The six prices add to $2,700K, so the mean is 2,700 ÷ 6 = $450K, matching the reporter — but the median is the average of the middle two prices, $195K and $200K, which is $197.5K. Five of the six homes cost between $180K and $210K, so the $1,725K home is an outlier pulling the mean far above what most homes cost. The claim is misleading, and the median better represents a typical price.
onLevel.explanationEs: Los seis precios suman $2,700K, así que la media es 2,700 ÷ 6 = $450K, igual que dice el reportero; pero la mediana es el promedio de los dos precios del medio, $195K y $200K, o sea $197.5K. Cinco de las seis casas cuestan entre $180K y $210K, así que la casa de $1,725K es un valor atípico que jala la media muy por encima de lo que cuestan casi todas. La afirmación es engañosa, y la mediana representa mejor un precio típico.

extending.stem: A scout records points per game: 14, 16, 15, 17, 16, 58. To report a TYPICAL game, which measure of center is best?
choices: Median, because 58 is an outlier that pulls the mean up
Mean, because it uses every game
Range, because it shows the highest game
Mode, because 16 appears twice
extending.explanation: The 58-point game is an outlier. It pulls the mean above 5 of the 6 games, so the median (16) better shows a typical game.
choiceFeedback: The mean is pulled higher by 58—does that show a typical game?
Range is 44—does that describe typical, or spread?
16 appears twice—is mode about a typical game when there's an outlier?
extending.stemEs: Un observador registra los puntos por partido: 14, 16, 15, 17, 16, 58. Para informar un partido TÍPICO, ¿cuál medida de centro es la mejor?
extending.explanationEs: El partido de 58 puntos es un valor atípico. Jala la media por encima de 5 de los 6 partidos, así que la mediana (16) muestra mejor un partido típico.
hints: A typical value should sit near most of the data instead of being pulled by one unusual game.
Scan for an outlier first, then choose the measure that an outlier does not drag around.
Put the scores in order: 14, 15, 16, 16, 17, 58. Compare where the middle of that list sits to where the average of all six would land.
hintsEs: Un valor típico debe quedar cerca de la mayoría de los datos y no ser jalado por un solo partido poco común.
Busca primero un valor atípico y después elige la medida que un valor atípico no arrastra.
Ordena las puntuaciones: 14, 15, 16, 16, 17, 58. Compara dónde queda el centro de esa lista con dónde caería el promedio de los seis.

extending.stem: The equipment manager needs to order the MOST COMMON jersey size from this list: M, L, M, S, M, L, M. Which measure answers the question?
choices: Mode, because it names the value that appears most
Mean, because it averages the sizes
Median, because it finds the middle size
Range, because it shows the size gap
extending.explanation: The mode is the value that shows up most often. Here size M appears 4 times, so the mode (M) tells the manager what to order most.
choiceFeedback: Average size doesn't make sense—which size appears most?
Median finds the middle order—which size shows up most?
Range is the spread—which size do you order most?
extending.stemEs: El encargado del equipo necesita pedir la talla de camiseta MÁS COMÚN de esta lista: M, L, M, S, M, L, M. ¿Cuál medida responde la pregunta?
extending.explanationEs: La moda es el valor que aparece con más frecuencia. Aquí la talla M aparece 4 veces, así que la moda (M) le dice al encargado qué pedir en mayor cantidad.
hints: Sizes like S, M, and L are categories, not numbers you can add or average.
Ask which measure of center reports the value that appears most often.
Count how many times each size shows up in M, L, M, S, M, L, M and see which count comes out largest.
hintsEs: Las tallas como S, M y L son categorías, no números que se puedan sumar o promediar.
Pregúntate cuál medida de centro informa el valor que aparece con más frecuencia.
Cuenta cuántas veces aparece cada talla en M, L, M, S, M, L, M y observa cuál conteo resulta mayor.

extending.stem: A coach wants to know how SPREAD OUT the team's free-throw makes are: 6, 7, 6, 8, 18. Which measure of spread is most affected by the lone 18?
choices: Range, because it is the highest minus the lowest value
Median, because it is in the middle
Mode, because it is the most common
Mean absolute deviation only, never the range
extending.explanation: Range = max − min = 18 − 6 = 12. Because it uses only the two most extreme values, one outlier (18) changes the range a lot.
choiceFeedback: Median finds middle—does it measure spread?
Mode is most common—does it measure spread?
MAD measures spread—but range is most affected by one extreme value.
extending.stemEs: Un entrenador quiere saber qué tan DISPERSOS están los tiros libres encestados del equipo: 6, 7, 6, 8, 18. ¿Cuál medida de dispersión se ve más afectada por el único 18?
extending.explanationEs: Rango = máximo − mínimo = 18 − 6 = 12. Como usa solamente los dos valores más extremos, un solo valor atípico (18) cambia mucho el rango.
hints: Measures of spread describe how far apart the values are, not where the center sits.
Look for the measure that is calculated from only the largest and the smallest values.
Compare the data with the 18 and without it, and notice which calculation changes the moment that value is removed.
hintsEs: Las medidas de dispersión describen qué tan separados están los valores, no dónde está el centro.
Busca la medida que se calcula usando solamente el valor mayor y el menor.
Compara los datos con el 18 y sin él, y fíjate cuál cálculo cambia en el momento en que se quita ese valor.

extending.title: Level 2 Extension — The Analyst's Wrong Measure

workedExample.label: Data
workedExample.work: A player's points per game: 19, 21, 20, 22, 23, 2 (the 2 was a game cut short by an early ejection).

workedExample.label: Analyst's choice
workedExample.work: The analyst reports the mean (17.8) as the player's typical scoring because it uses all the data.

extending.correctWork: The analyst should report the median (20.5), not the mean. The score of 2 is an outlier from the cut-short game. It pulls the mean down to 17.8, which is lower than 5 of the 6 games, so it does not represent a typical performance. The median (20.5) is resistant to the outlier and better describes a typical game.
hints: Look at the value 2. Does it fit with the rest of the player's scores, or is it an outlier?
The mean (17.8) is lower than 5 of the 6 games. A good 'typical' value should sit among most of the data, like the median (20.5) does.
extending.titleEs: Extensión de Nivel 2: la medida equivocada del analista
extending.explanation: The 2-point game was cut short by an ejection, so it is an outlier, and it drags the mean down to about 17.8 — lower than five of the six games. The median 20.5 sits among the 19-to-23 point games, so it describes the player's typical scoring much better.
extending.explanationEs: El partido de 2 puntos se acortó por una expulsión, así que es un valor atípico, y jala la media hasta cerca de 17.8, más bajo que cinco de los seis partidos. La mediana 20.5 queda entre los partidos de 19 a 23 puntos, así que describe mucho mejor la anotación típica del jugador.

extending.stem: A gymnast's scores are: 8.5, 8.8, 8.7, 8.6, 8.9. There are no outliers. Which measure best represents a typical score?
choices: Mean
Median
Neither — the data is too small
Both are equally bad
extending.explanation: The data is symmetric with no outliers, so the mean (8.7) best represents the typical score.
choiceFeedback: The median ignores how far apart the values are. Check whether this data has any outlier that would make leaving values out worthwhile.
Five values is plenty for a measure of center. A small set is only a problem when it contains extreme values.
Both measures actually work reasonably well here, since the scores are clustered close together. Decide which one uses the data most fully when there are no outliers.
hints: Look at the scores: 8.5 up to 8.9 — all five are bunched tightly together with no unusual value.
Rule of thumb: with no outliers and balanced data, one measure uses every value fairly. With outliers, the middle value is safer. Which case is this?
First step: check for an outlier — is any score far from the others? All five sit within 0.4 points, so apply the no-outlier rule.
extending.stemEs: Las puntuaciones de una gimnasta son: 8.5, 8.8, 8.7, 8.6, 8.9. No hay valores atípicos. ¿Cuál medida representa mejor una puntuación típica?
extending.explanationEs: Los datos son simétricos y no tienen valores atípicos, así que la media (8.7) representa mejor la puntuación típica.

extending.stem: A runner's mile times are: 7:10, 7:15, 7:12, 7:20, 12:00. The 12:00 was due to a cramp. Which measure best represents a typical mile?
choices: Median — the outlier 12:00 pulls the mean too high
Mean — it uses all the data
Mode — it shows the most common time
Neither measure works
extending.explanation: The 12:00 is an outlier that pulls the mean up. The median (7:15) better represents the runner's typical time.
choiceFeedback: Mean uses all data—but the outlier pulls it too high.
Mode shows most common—but doesn't handle the outlier well.
Both measures exist, but which resists the 12:00 outlier?
hints: Four times are near 7 minutes; one is 12:00 from a cramp. That 12:00 is an outlier, not a typical mile.
Ask: which measure gets dragged toward an extreme value, and which one just takes the middle of the ordered list?
First step: order the times and notice where 12:00 sits — far beyond the rest. Then choose the measure that isn't pulled by that extreme time.
extending.stemEs: Los tiempos de una corredora en la milla son: 7:10, 7:15, 7:12, 7:20, 12:00. El 12:00 se debió a un calambre. ¿Cuál medida representa mejor una milla típica?
extending.explanationEs: El 12:00 es un valor atípico que sube la media. La mediana (7:15) representa mejor el tiempo típico de la corredora.

extending.stem: Data set: 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 50. The mean is about 13.8 and the median is 7. Which better represents the typical value?
choices: Median (7) — the outlier 50 inflates the mean
Mean (13.8) — it includes all values
Both are equally good
Neither works for this data
extending.explanation: The mean (13.8) is higher than 5 of the 6 values because the outlier 50 pulls it up. The median (7) better represents a typical value.
choiceFeedback: Mean uses all data—but 50 pulls it way above 5 of the 6 values.
Both exist, but which is closer to most of the data points?
One works well for typical value—use the one that resists 50.
hints: Five of the six values are between 5 and 8 — then there's 50. Notice where the mean (13.8) lands compared to those five.
Test for 'typical': count how many actual data values sit near 13.8, then how many sit near 7. A good measure stays close to most of the data.
First step: compare 13.8 to the list — it's bigger than 5, 6, 7, 7, AND 8. Ask what pulled it up there, and whether the median has that problem.
extending.stemEs: Conjunto de datos: 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 50. La media es aproximadamente 13.8 y la mediana es 7. ¿Cuál representa mejor el valor típico?
extending.explanationEs: La media (13.8) es mayor que 5 de los 6 valores porque el valor atípico 50 la jala hacia arriba. La mediana (7) representa mejor un valor típico.

extending.title: Spot the Mistake — Forgetting to Order the Data

workedExample.label: Find the median
workedExample.work: The student keeps the numbers as written (9, 12, 8, 11, 10) and picks the middle one: median = 8.

workedExample.label: Choose a measure
workedExample.work: The student reports the median (8) as the typical lap count.

extending.correctWork: You must put the data in order before finding the median. In order: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. The middle value is 10, so the median is 10 (not 8). Since there are no outliers, the mean (10) and median (10) agree, and either is a fine measure of a typical lap.
hints: The median is the MIDDLE value only after the numbers are sorted from least to greatest.
Sort the data first: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. Now which value sits in the middle?
extending.titleEs: Detecta el error: olvidar ordenar los datos
extending.explanation: The median is the middle value only after the data is sorted. Ordering 9, 12, 8, 11, 10 gives 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, so the median is 10 — the 8 that was reported is actually the smallest value in the set. With no outliers here, the mean is also 10, so either measure describes a typical lap count.
extending.explanationEs: La mediana es el valor del medio solo después de ordenar los datos. Ordenar 9, 12, 8, 11, 10 da 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, así que la mediana es 10; el 8 que se reportó en realidad es el valor más pequeño del conjunto. Como aquí no hay valores atípicos, la media también es 10, así que cualquiera de las dos medidas describe una cantidad típica de vueltas.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Appropriate Measures is defaulting to the mean just because "it uses all the data," without first checking whether an outlier or skewed shape is present. For example, given a player's points per game 14, 16, 15, 17, 16, 58, a student calculates the mean (136 ÷ 6 ≈ 22.7) and reports that as the typical game — but 58 is far from the cluster of 14–17, so it pulls the mean above 5 of the 6 games. The median (16) actually represents a typical game here. Before choosing a measure, always scan the data for an outlier or a long tail first: only use the mean once you've confirmed the data has neither.

diagram.title: The Six Playoff Ticket Prices
diagram.caption: One courtside outlier towers over the rest — it drags the mean up to $85 even though the median ticket costs about $51.

connect.scenario: A sports reporter writes: 'The average ticket price for the playoffs is $85.' The actual prices are: $45, $50, $48, $52, $55, $260. The $260 ticket is a courtside seat.
connect.promptQuestion: Is $85 a fair way to describe a 'typical' ticket price? What measure should the reporter use?
connect.prompt: The reporter used the ___, which is ___. A better measure would be the ___ (about ___) because ___. The courtside seat at $260 is an ___ that pulls the mean ___.

check.stem: What is the mean ticket price?
check.explanation: The six prices total $510, and 510 ÷ 6 = $85 — matching the reporter's claim.

check.stem: What is the median ticket price?
check.explanation: In order: 45, 48, 50, 52, 55, 260. With 6 values the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th: (50 + 52) ÷ 2 = $51.

check.stem: Which measure better describes a 'typical' ticket?
choices: The median, because the $260 outlier pulls the mean far above most prices
The mean, because it uses every value
Neither — you should use the mode
The mean, because $85 is between the extremes
check.explanation: Five of the six tickets cost between $45 and $55. The single $260 courtside seat drags the mean up to $85, higher than every ordinary ticket. The median of $51 sits right where most prices actually are.

connect.modelAnswer: The reporter used the mean, $85 — but five of the six tickets cost between $45 and $55, so $85 is higher than almost every real ticket. The $260 courtside seat is an outlier that pulls the mean upward. The median, about $51, describes a typical ticket far better because it is not affected by one extreme value.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — Data set: 15, 18, 16, 17, 15, 72. Which measure of center best represents the data?
choices: Median, because 72 is an outlier
Mean, because it uses all values
Mean, because it is always best
Neither works for this data
exitTicket.explanation: The value 72 is an outlier. The mean (25.5) is pulled high by 72 and doesn't represent the typical values. The median (16.5) is a better measure of center.
choiceFeedback: True, but 72 pulls the mean up — an outlier distorts it.
Not always — a big outlier like 72 makes the median better.
One does work — the median resists the outlier 72.
hints: Scan the data: five values sit between 15 and 18, then one is 72. Ask yourself what that 72 does to an average.
One measure adds every value, so the 72 counts fully; the other uses only the middle of the ordered list. Decide which stays near most values.
First step: order the six values and locate the middle two — notice 72 sits at the far end. Then think about where the mean would land.

questions.stem: A data set has absolute deviations of 3, 1, 5, 2, 4. What is the MAD?
The mean of a data set is 20. A value is 26. What is the absolute deviation?
Team A has MAD = 2.1 points. Team B has MAD = 6.8 points. Which team is more consistent?
choices: Team B — higher MAD means better performance
Both are equally consistent
Team A — lower MAD means scores are closer to the mean
Cannot tell from MAD alone
questions.explanation: Lower MAD means less spread — Team A's scores stay closer to their average, making them more consistent.
